The Four Product Risks

Value, usability, feasibility, viability — and why the useful question is not which risk is largest but which is cheapest to settle now and most expensive to meet later.

1. Two decisions, seventeen days apart

On Tuesday, 13 January 2026, Ridhima Thiruvengadam sat with a board note she did not believe. She was vice-president of product at Xynova Credit Technologies, a Bengaluru firm selling to non-banking financial companies — the mid-sized lenders who write two-wheeler and small-business loans in towns the large private banks do not staff. Xynova's proposal, Xolve Underwrite, read a borrower's bank statements, pay slips and bureau report and handed the credit officer a recommended decision with reason codes. The board had sanctioned ₹360 lakh over nine months — the team's burn of ₹40 lakh a month multiplied out — with seven weeks of discovery first.

Her engineering lead, Riyaz Tulsiani, wanted those weeks spent extending his extraction spike. A preliminary run on already-digitised statements had returned 96.2 per cent per field; but co-operative-bank statements arrive as photographs of printouts, and he put the odds of missing the target there at two in five. The chief executive wanted letters of intent. Thiruvengadam's worry was duller. The price in the note was ₹18 per application decisioned, set just under what a lender pays for a bureau pull, and nobody had computed what a decisioned application would cost to produce. It was not anyone's job.

Seventeen days later Rameez Tanwar had the opposite problem. Tanwar led product at Xyrata Devices in Pune, maker of a reusable cold-chain logger that rides inside a pharmaceutical carton and alerts a companion phone app when the carton leaves its 2–8 °C band. Xyrata had quoted a distributor for 900 units: ₹57.60 lakh of hardware at ₹6,400 each, plus subscription at ₹1,150 a device. A one-month pilot across three distributors had just closed, and the engineering risks had not materialised: battery life measured 71 days against a 60-day specification, packet loss 2.1 per cent. The devices had raised 61 excursion alerts. Tanwar asked, almost idly, how many produced a documented corrective action — somebody moving a carton into a working chamber. Nine. Two product types, one question: of all the things that must be true, which do we falsify first? The four product risks are the standard answer, and the distance between a competent use of them and an expert one lies almost entirely in what the boxes do not contain.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

The four product risks classify the conditions that must hold for a product to succeed, partitioned by who can settle each condition and with what kind of evidence. Value risk is the chance customers will not choose it. Usability risk is the chance customers who want it cannot work out how to use it. Feasibility risk is the chance the team cannot build it with the technology, skills, data, time and money available. Viability risk is the chance the business around it cannot sustain it — on cost, price, law, brand, operations or strategy.

IDEO had long taught a triad of desirability, feasibility and viability, popularised in Tim Brown's Change by Design (2009). Marty Cagan, at HP, Netscape and eBay before founding the Silicon Valley Product Group, split desirability in two in Inspired (2008, rewritten 2017) and gave each risk an owner: the product manager owns value and viability, the designer usability, the engineering lead feasibility. The target was organisational. In a requirements-driven firm, value and viability were settled by a stakeholder before the team existed, so the team's cheap early weeks went to the one risk it was permitted to touch — feasibility, also the risk engineers find most interesting. Blank (2005), Ries (2011) and, earlier, McGrath and MacMillan’s “Discovery-Driven Planning” (Harvard Business Review, 1995) attacked the same target; that paper’s assumption checklist is the ancestor of the claim ledger below.

One structural point makes the rest legible. A proposal is a conjunction of claims, and conjunctions decay fast. Five independent claims each 85 per cent likely leave the conjunction at 44.4 per cent. Xynova's five claims, at the probabilities the team elicited in week one, multiply out to 9.2 per cent — but only if the claims are independent, and they are not. The compliance and value claims move together, and positive correlation pushes the true joint probability above 9.2 per cent. The correction does not rescue the proposal: nobody had multiplied anything at all, and the board was about to commit ₹360 lakh without knowing the order of magnitude.

3. Mechanics: the claim ledger and the ranking nobody runs

One: write the idea as falsifiable claims with thresholds attached — not “lenders want this” but “two of three design partners sign a paid pilot within six weeks” — because a threshold written after the test is a rationalisation. Two: assign each claim to a risk, and treat the argument about the assignment as the useful output. When Tulsiani said “credit officers won't trust the reason codes,” three people assigned that sentence to three boxes: a usability claim about whether reason codes are legible, a value claim about whether a lender buys a tool its officers distrust, and a viability claim about whether a board-approved credit policy can accommodate a model-assisted decision. Three claims, three tests, one sentence; half the framework's benefit is forcing it apart.

Three: estimate three parameters per claim, not one. The probability it is false, p; the build spend committed between the moment a test could settle it and the moment it would announce its own falsity unaided, the avoidable loss A; and the cost of the test now, c.

Four: rank by net expected value of information, p × A − c. All five of Xynova's tests resolve inside the same seven-week pre-build window, so the spend before any resolves is common and cancels out; A is the ₹40 lakh monthly burn times the months from the start of the build to unaided discovery.

The ranking is the finding. By probability of being false — the plain reading of “riskiest assumption first,” this topic's prerequisite and its commonest oversimplification — the order is unit economics, feasibility, usability, compliance, value. By net value of information it is unit economics, usability, compliance, value, feasibility. Feasibility moves from second to last, not because it is unlikely to fail but because it fails early, loudly and cheaply: a four-month extraction failure costs ₹160 lakh of avoidable spend, a month-eight usability failure twice that. For the spike to regain second place Tulsiani's claim would need p(false) above 0.71, since 0.71 × 160 − 6 is about the usability test's net of 108. He put it at 0.40.

Five, the step with the second-order effect: run the free test first regardless of rank. The unit-economics claim cost ₹2 lakh — a spreadsheet and two days of a finance analyst — carried the highest net value of information, and had not been run, because it belonged to no function: the engineers did not price, and finance did not model products that did not exist. Naming owners, Cagan's great practical contribution, means a claim falling between two owners is a claim nobody writes down — the framework's engine and its blind spot in one move.

4. The conditions, stated so they could be false

One: the four decompose only if their repairs differ. At Xynova they do: a value failure kills the product, a usability failure changes the interface, a compliance failure changes the contract. At Xyrata they nearly do not — the usability failure in the alert chain and the viability failure in the customer's profit and loss are one fact seen from two sides.

Two: discovery pays only when c is small relative to p × A. On a two-week build — ₹20 lakh at Xynova's burn — the unit-economics test still clears (0.55 × 20 − 2 = ₹9 lakh) but the usability test barely does (0.35 × 20 − 4 = ₹3 lakh). A four-risk sweep on a two-week build performs diligence rather than exercising it.

The framework actively misleads in three situations: when the real risk is distribution, since a product can clear all four boxes and die because nobody can reach the customer below what the customer is worth; when the value a test observes is produced by scaffolding the team means to remove; and in a new category, where asking whether people want what they have never seen answers about the question, not the product.

5. Hard edges: two-sided, regulated, physical, AI-native, and the seams

Two-sided products split value risk in two, and the halves cannot be tested at once. In a four-week marketplace pilot Xynova's chief executive had run earlier, buyers made 1,200 searches; 318 of those searches returned at least three live quotes, which is 26.5 per cent; and 86 of the 318 fillable searches converted, which is 27.0 per cent. End to end, 86 of 1,200 searches transacted, or 7.2 per cent, and a board reading only that concludes buyers do not want the product. The decomposition says the opposite: given supply, better than one fillable search in four converted. The failure is liquidity, which sits in no box and is repaired by a supply operation, not a product change. Note the base: 1,200 is searches, not buyers.

In regulated products viability is binary and must be tested out of order. Most risks admit partial credit; a credit committee's refusal does not. Thiruvengadam's compliance claim ranked third and she ran it second, because a calendar she did not control has a latency the arithmetic ignores.

In hardware-plus-software, feasibility risk is time-asymmetric, and the asymmetry dominates the loss. Xyrata's enclosure needed an injection-moulding tool: ₹46 lakh and fourteen weeks of lead time. A software failure found in week fifteen costs a sprint; a tooling decision found wrong then costs the tool and the fourteen weeks again. Ranking must weight irreversibility and not only rupees — which is why hardware teams run feasibility first even when value of information says otherwise, and are usually right to.

In AI-native products feasibility becomes a rate, and the rate compounds. Tulsiani's preliminary spike returned 96.2 per cent accuracy per extracted field on digitised statements, which the team read as past its 96 per cent threshold. Xolve Underwrite extracts fourteen fields per application, seven bearing on the adjudication.

At the organisational seams, mature companies do not do what they say. The published answer is a trio owning all four risks jointly. The observed answer, at Xyrata's size, is that the device team owned the sensor, the app team the notification, sales the quality head who signed, and nobody the warehouse loader with a shared handset at eleven at night. Seventeen of the 61 alerts went to a phone off, locked or in someone else's pocket — a claim on no risk list, because it was not a property of anything anyone owned.

6. Five distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: the probability a claim is false is the least useful of its three parameters. Everyone estimates p because it feels like the risky part. The expert asks first when the claim would announce itself unaided, and what will have been spent by then. The tell-tale is a plan that defers the most-likely-to-fail claim on purpose, with a written reason; the obvious reading is wrong because some failures are self-reporting and some stay silent for years.

Two: value and usability failure share their top-line telemetry and diverge on the second session. Both look like low adoption, so the expert asks what the same user did on the second occasion: a value failure never returns, a usability failure returns and fails again in the same place. The tell-tale is a team that has cohorted by attempt rather than by week. Its business-product cousin is the separation of buyer from user — the buyer a quality head with an incentive, the user a loader with a shared handset and a queue — so the expert asks who holds the device and whether anything rewards them for responding. A usability test recruited by the buyer tested the wrong person.

Three: viability is the risk with no natural champion, which is why it is tested last and kills most often. Value has a product manager, usability a designer, feasibility an engineer; viability has a spreadsheet, and the tell-tale is reliably comic: the cheapest test on the board is the one nobody has run.

Four: in AI products, per-unit accuracy is not system accuracy, and the conversion is the first thing an expert does. Faced with “96.2 per cent,” the expert asks “accurate per what, and how many per transaction?” before judging the number; the tell-tale is a specification quoting an accuracy without naming its unit. The second-order effect bites hardest: residual error does not vanish, it becomes a human-review queue, turning a feasibility number into a unit-cost number and moving the risk between boxes unnoticed.

Five: a test can validate its own scaffolding, and the four boxes have no room for distribution. Concierge and Wizard-of-Oz tests put a human where a system will later be, and the human improvises; if the improvisation is what the customer valued, the test measured something the product will not contain. The expert asks what in a test will not exist at scale, and whether that was load-bearing — the tell-tale being feedback that names a person, not a feature. The parallel absence is growth, answered by Ries's growth hypothesis, Teresa Torres's ethical assumption class (2021) and Bland and Osterwalder's Testing Business Ideas (2019), and written by the expert as a fifth line on the board.

7. What changes by product type and stage, and what does not

The sharpest real difference is the statistical tractability of value risk, and it is a difference of kind. A consumer team can settle a value claim with a powered experiment: detecting a two-percentage-point absolute lift on a four per cent baseline at 80 per cent power and five per cent two-sided significance needs about (1.96 + 0.84)2 × [0.04 × 0.96 + 0.06 × 0.94] ÷ 0.022 = 1,858 per arm; halve the effect and the requirement more than triples, to 6,735. Xynova's universe is perhaps 340 lenders — a working estimate, and the conclusion holds at many times it — so no arm size makes a statistical value test possible — which is why enterprise value evidence is necessarily ordinal: letters of intent, deposits, paid pilots with a kill clause.

Stage changes the binding constraint, not the risk. At seed value dominates, and the characteristic failure is being unable to run a viability test at all, because it needs a counterparty — a bank, a regulator, a distributor — who will not take the meeting. At growth stage the dominant risk inverts: revenue has answered the value question, and the usual error is to keep running value tests on a product demonstrably wanted and quietly unprofitable. Two claimed differences are not real: usability risk does not differ in kind between consumer and business products, only in who holds the device, and feasibility risk at seed and at scale is one risk with two balance sheets behind it.

Two: nine of sixty-one (Xyrata, usability presenting as viability)

Tanwar instrumented the alert chain across the pilot's 61 excursions. The flattering rate — 26 of the 44 alerts that reached someone on shift were acknowledged inside the 30-minute service level, which is 59.1 per cent — is the wrong denominator. A carton spoils whether or not its alert found a handset, so the business claim is measured over all 61.

End to end, 9 of 61 excursions produced the action the product exists to cause, which is 14.8 per cent, against a specification of 90 per cent acknowledged and 70 per cent acted on — a design intent of 63.0 per cent. The ordinary interval around 14.8 per cent on 61 observations is roughly plus or minus 8.9 points, giving 5.9 to 23.7 per cent; the true interval is wider, because alerts cluster within site and consignment, and three sites cannot support an honest estimate of that clustering, so no design effect is quoted. Its upper bound still sits forty points below the design intent. The usability number is also the viability number, and that is the lesson: the distributor ships 1,80,000 cartons a year, of which 0.9 per cent suffer a spoiling excursion — 1,620 cartons at ₹4,100 each, or ₹66.42 lakh of annual loss.

Three: where the method failed, and what recovery cost (Xylora Fresh, consumer)

Xylora Fresh, a Hyderabad subscription business, ran a textbook sweep on Xobi, a weekly fruit-and-vegetable box with a recipe plan. Between February and April 2025 a 12-week concierge pilot served 220 households, with 172 of 220 still subscribed at week four, which is 78.2 per cent. Usability passed; feasibility was never in doubt; contribution modelled positive at ₹680 a box against ₹497 of goods and delivery, or ₹183 a box. Rajat Thimmaiah in product and Roma Talegaonkar in finance recommended launch, and on any reading of the four risks they had done the work. The launch cohort ran July to November 2025: 3,180 households, of whom 1,304 of 3,180 were still subscribed at week four, which is 41.0 per cent. The pilot's rate predicts 2,486 retained; the 1,182-household shortfall, at ₹840 of acquisition cost each, is ₹9.93 lakh spent on households already gone.

The framework had not been misapplied; it had been applied to the wrong object. In the pilot a human telephoned each household when an item was unavailable, proposed a substitute and talked about the week's recipes. That call was scaffolding, scheduled for removal. It was also, it turned out, the product. The four risks told Thimmaiah to test value, and he did, honestly and well; nothing in them told him the value he measured was produced by the part he meant to delete.

9. Four failure modes, with their early warnings

Testing the risk owned by the loudest competent person, or running the sweep as a gate rather than a ranking. Warning: the plan's first item is a technical spike, or it has four equal workstreams. Diagnostic: “if we could run exactly one test, which?” Late cost: a seven-week plan whose value and feasibility workstreams carried nets of ₹61 lakh and ₹58 lakh — ₹119 lakh between them — while the unscheduled two-day spreadsheet carried ₹196 lakh.

Validating the scaffolding. Warning: a human sits in a loop you intend to automate, improvising. Diagnostic: “what here will not exist at scale, and was it load-bearing?” Late cost: Xylora's 37-point retention gap and ₹9.93 lakh of acquisition spend on households already gone.

Naming the wrong denominator. Warning: a funnel whose stages have different bases, or a rate whose clock starts elsewhere than its numerator's. Diagnostic: “how many units were eligible here, and is the window the numerator's?” Late cost: Xyrata nearly shipped on 59.1 per cent when the governing number was 14.8 per cent.

Mistaking a seam for a box. Warning: every risk has an owner and the owners' lists are disjoint. Diagnostic: “which claim is on nobody's list?” Late cost: Xyrata's 17 undelivered alerts — nobody's risk, because the shared handset was nobody's component.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Four risks or three? The discovery school splits desirability because value and usability fail, are diagnosed and are repaired differently, and merging them produces onboarding redesigns for unwanted products. The design school answers that usability is craft, not risk: you do not run a go/no-go test on legibility. For the split to be wrong, the two failures would have to lead to the same action — and sometimes they do, as at Xyrata, where the usability defect and the viability defect were one fact with two names. Separability is contingent, which makes the right number of boxes a property of the situation rather than of the framework.

Riskiest assumption first, or highest value of information first? The riskiest-assumption camp has a serious epistemic argument: p is the one parameter a team can estimate honestly, while A and c are guesses, and a value-of-information table launders two guesses into a number carrying the authority of arithmetic. The decision-analytic camp has Xynova's table, where the ranking inverts robustly — Tulsiani's claim would have to be nearly twice as likely to fail before the naive order returned. Riskiest-first is right when A is roughly equal across claims: true in short-build software, false in hardware and in anything whose failure can stay silent for eight months.

Is value risk testable at all before you build? The sceptical position, with jobs-to-be-done sympathies and a literature on stated versus revealed preference behind it, is that every pre-build value test measures an opinion or a purchase of something that does not exist, and so tells you about your test. The constructive position is that the evidence ladder answers this: a deposit, an intent letter, a pilot signed with a cancellation clause are revealed preference with money attached. For the ladder to be theatre, deposit-backed demand would have to fail to predict post-launch demand — and there is no good public dataset on the predictive validity of pre-sale evidence. Both sides reason from their own portfolios; this is open.

Who owns viability? Cagan holds that viability decisions are product decisions, and a product manager who outsources them ships products the company cannot sell. Finance leaders answer, with justice, that the product manager has neither the information nor the incentive: fully loaded cost, cost of capital and the true cost of a 33-seat voice operation are not on their desk, and Xylora's ₹430-versus-₹640 error is an instance. The strongest reading of both is that the product manager must own the claim and must not own the number — a division of labour neither school states cleanly.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied the four risks names them correctly and produces a two-by-two with four tests in it. Someone who has internalised them converts every accuracy or rate claim into an end-to-end figure before judging it; asks when each claim would announce itself unaided, and defers the likeliest failure on purpose and in writing; runs the free test first even when dull, the dull test being usually the unowned one; writes thresholds before tests, treating one moved afterwards as a finding about the team; names the denominator out loud; and says “I do not know which risk this is” without embarrassment, because the ambiguity names the claims still unwritten. Studio courses at Berkeley, Stanford and Cornell Tech build the habit by making teams test a material assumption on a real product.

12. What each of them decided

Thiruvengadam reordered rather than reduced. In week one she ran the ₹2 lakh model, found the ₹3.24 loss per application, and took a per-approved-loan price of ₹140 to three design-partner lenders; two signed paid pilots at the new structure. In week two she ran the committee sign-off claim, which had no partial credit and a counterparty calendar she did not control; the usability test ran in weeks three to five. The vernacular extraction claim — the open half of Tulsiani's spike — was deferred into the build on the written ground that it would surface by month four at an avoidable loss of ₹160 lakh. The board's decision changed shape: not a ₹360 lakh commitment, but ₹120 lakh to month three, three months of burn, with a kill threshold on the review-queue rate — a rate that rests on the preliminary spike and will move when the vernacular sample lands.

Tanwar did not run the battery spike his team had asked for; the pilot had settled it. He spent three weeks instrumenting the alert chain, and the repair was not in the app: a named shift owner for the handset, a display in the cold room, escalation to a supervisor at twenty minutes. He withdrew the 900-device quote and replaced it with a 120-device, 90-day paid deployment — ₹7.68 lakh of hardware and ₹34,500 of subscription for the quarter — carrying a contractual measurement of the save rate, since a customer who cannot verify one cannot renew on it. His sales director objected that the deal had shrunk from 900 devices to 120. Tanwar's answer was that the 900-device deal had a negative net present value for the buyer and would not have renewed.

  1. Thiruvengadam deferred the claim her team rated second most likely to fail. On what evidence would you overrule her, and what would you give up to run that spike inside the seven weeks?
  2. Xyrata's defect appeared in the customer's capital case, not in Xyrata's product metrics. What instrument, installed before the pilot, would have surfaced it in week one — and who would have owned it?
  3. Xylora's recovery restores the margin and installs a 33-seat voice operation. Is that a product decision, a viability decision or a change of business model — and which risk, if any, should have caught it?

The Four Product Risks

Value, usability, feasibility, viability: finding the one that could kill the product, and testing it first.

1. A Monday in August

On Monday, 3 August 2026, Parnika Sethi, head of product at Xelmar Wholesale, opened a spreadsheet that her chief executive wanted answered by the board meeting on 14 August. Xelmar, a distributor of packaged staples (flour, oil, tea, detergent) to roughly 9,000 neighbourhood kirana stores around Pune and Nashik, had proposed a product called Xinara: a phone app in which a shopkeeper could dictate a restocking order in Hindi or Marathi and have it delivered the next morning. The board had approved a build budget of ₹240 lakh (₹2.4 crore) over nine months for a team of eleven.

The proposal read well. Sales representatives said shopkeepers hated phoning in orders. Two engineers had built a demonstration in which a spoken sentence became a shopping list. The chief executive, Pratap Shirke, wanted a go decision. Sethi's concern was narrower and more uncomfortable: she could not say which of the many things that had to be true was most likely to be false. Was it that shopkeepers would not change habits? That they could not use the app with flour on their hands? That speech recognition would fail on a Nashik accent? Or that Xelmar would lose money on every order it delivered?

If she chose badly, the cost was concrete. A team spending ₹240 lakh to build the wrong thing discovers the fault in month seven, not in week two. Her task, in effect, was to decide what to find out first. The risk classification itself is well established; the way of ranking the tests that this page builds up from Sethi's spreadsheet is a heuristic of the author's own, and is labelled as such where it appears.

2. The idea

The four product risks are a classification of the ways a product idea can fail. Value risk is the chance that customers will not want it enough to choose it. Usability risk is the chance that customers who do want it cannot work out how to use it. Feasibility risk is the chance that the team cannot build it with the technology, skills, time and money available. Viability risk is the chance that the business cannot sustain it: that it fails on cost, law, brand, operations or the strategy of the company around it.

The framework was invented to solve a recurring and costly habit: teams treat building as the hard part, and so spend their early effort on the one risk (feasibility) that engineers find most interesting. Marty Cagan, a product leader who worked at eBay and Netscape before founding the consultancy SVPG, set out these four risks in his writing from about 2008 onward, and assigned them to the product trio: the product manager owns value and viability, the designer owns usability, the engineering lead owns feasibility. A similar triad of desirability, feasibility and viability had earlier been used by the design firm IDEO; Cagan's contribution was to split desirability into value and usability, because the two fail differently and are repaired differently.

Sethi's sentence for the meeting: “Four different things can kill this, and we should find out which one is most likely, cheapest to check, and most expensive to be wrong about before we spend the money.”

Each box contains a question that can be answered yes or no by evidence, and a test that produces the evidence. A risk with no test attached is still an opinion. The figure also shows that the four boxes ask about four different parties: the customer's wish, the customer's hands, the engineers' tools and the company's ledger.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, two of which practitioners usually leave unspoken. First, write down the assumptions that must hold for the idea to succeed, phrased so that they can be false: “at least 30 per cent of trial stores will place a second order unprompted” rather than “shopkeepers will like it”. Second, sort each assumption into one of the four risks. Sorting is less trivial than it sounds; the useful test is to ask what the failure would look like. If the shopkeeper says “I do not need this”, the risk is value. If she says “I could not find the button”, it is usability.

Third, and this is the implicit step, estimate for each risk how likely it is to be fatal, and how much would be lost if it were discovered late. These estimates are judgments, and they should be written down and argued over, because the argument is the point. Fourth, price the cheapest credible test for each. Fifth, run first the test that offers the most exposure removed per rupee spent, subject to one more implicit step: check whether any test is a precondition for another, since there is no point measuring ordering behaviour on a product that cannot recognise the orders.

Sethi's team spent two days on the first three steps. They listed twenty-two assumptions and found that most clustered under four: shopkeepers want to reorder by voice (value); can finish an order with a phone in one hand (usability); speech recognition reaches 90 per cent line-item accuracy across Marathi, Hindi and mixed speech (feasibility); and Xelmar can deliver at a positive margin (viability). Their cheapest tests, with costs, appear in Table 2 below.

4. A worked example, line by line

Take the viability risk first, because it is the one that needs only a spreadsheet. Sethi's pitch to the board assumed a gross margin of 6.5 per cent on an average order of ₹2,800. A call to the finance team revealed that distributor terms on the staples that shopkeepers reorder most often supported only 4.5 per cent. Delivery to a store cost ₹95 per order and payment fees and support ₹30, so the cost to serve was ₹125. A shopkeeper was assumed to order eight times a month, and winning one cost ₹900 in sales visits and onboarding.

On the pitch assumptions the product repays a store's acquisition cost in just under two months. On the distributor's actual terms it takes 112.5 months, about 9.4 years, which for a store account is effectively never. This single comparison is why viability risk, which no one had listed first, now looked like the likeliest killer. It did not show that Xinara was doomed. To repay acquisition in four months, a store must yield ₹225 a month (₹900 ÷ 4), or ₹28.125 per order across eight orders. Now the ranking. For each risk, Sethi's team estimated the probability that it was fatal, the value at stake if it were found late, and the cheapest test. The value at stake is the money that would already be spent if the fault surfaced late. Section 1 put discovery in month seven of nine, so the base is 7/9 of ₹240 lakh, or ₹186.67 lakh, used for value, feasibility and viability because each can kill the whole product. For usability it is 40 per cent of that, ₹74.67 lakh, on the assumption that a failed design can be rebuilt rather than abandoned. Exposure is probability times value at stake; the final column divides exposure by the test cost. This ratio is the author's heuristic, not an established method, and it assumes that a test removes all of its risk, which no real test does: a passed test lowers a probability, it does not set it to zero.

The point of this heuristic is not that viability always dominates; it is that the cheapness of a test matters as much as the size of the risk. A desk check that costs three days will often beat a field trial that costs three weeks.

Now change one input. Suppose the finance call had come back differently: Xelmar had already signed a sourcing agreement guaranteeing a 6.0 per cent margin on the staples shopkeepers reorder most. Gross margin would be 0.06 × 2,800 = ₹168, contribution ₹168 − ₹125 = ₹43 per order, ₹344 a month at eight orders, and acquisition cost would be recovered in 900 ÷ 344 = 2.62 months, comfortably inside the four-month target (which needed only ₹28.125 per order). Ranking governs the sequence and the stopping rule, not whether to test.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

The risks are not equally recoverable

A usability failure can usually be repaired by redesign; a value failure usually cannot, because no interface can make people want something they do not. This is why Table 2 charges usability only 40 per cent of the at-stake base. Treat that percentage as an input to argue about, not a constant.

Value and usability are routinely confused

When a test participant abandons a task, two explanations are available: she did not want what the task produced, or she could not operate it. A shopkeeper who stops halfway through a voice order may be confused, or may have realised she prefers her phone call to the sales representative, who also tells her which stock is cheap this week. The cheapest separator is to ask afterwards whether she would want the outcome if someone else did the typing.

Feasibility has two meanings

It can mean “can this be built at all” or “can it be built to the required quality, within this budget and date”. Speech recognition for Marathi exists; whether it reaches the required accuracy on noisy shop-floor audio is the real question. The unit scored matters: here it is the line item, not the utterance. The 400 recorded orders are assumed to average five line items each, 2,000 in all, and the pass mark is 1,800 correct (90 per cent). Scoring whole utterances would be a harsher and different test. Engineers answering the first meaning will report “yes” and mislead everyone.

Viability is wider than money

Margin is the commonest viability test, but legal, brand and operational constraints belong here too. If Xinara later offers shopkeepers credit on orders, the digital lending directions of the Reserve Bank of India become part of the viability question. These risks are checked by asking finance, counsel and operations, not the customer.

The risks interact

Batching deliveries to close the ₹27 cost gap means orders arrive in a two-hour window rather than on demand, which may weaken the value proposition. A test of one risk therefore sometimes changes the probability of another. Revisit the estimates after each result.

What the framework cannot tell you

It does not discover risks you have not thought of; it only sorts those you have. It does not turn judgments into probabilities; the 35 per cent and 25 per cent in Table 2 are opinions with a number attached, and the ranking built on them is a heuristic, not a law. And it does not tell you what to build. A newcomer should ask before relying on it: who produced these probabilities, and would a sceptic have chosen the same? Which assumption would I regret not having written down?

6. How it looks in different settings

SettingWhich risk tends to dominateWhy

Table 4. Tendencies, not rules. Xinara is B2B in the sense that shopkeepers are businesses, but consumer-like in that each shopkeeper is the sole decision-maker.

Xelmar sits awkwardly between rows, and that is typical. Its shopkeepers buy for themselves in minutes, so the sales cycle is consumer-short, yet the economics are B2B: a long-lived account is worth far more than one order. A small company has little to protect; one of Xelmar's size has a reputation among nine thousand stores, and so more to lose through viability and brand.

7. Common mistakes

Testing the comfortable risk. Symptom: two months of engineering prototypes and no conversation with a shopkeeper. Misunderstanding: that the risk you know how to test is the risk that matters. Diagnostic: ask the team which of the four risks has not yet had a test designed, and why.

Mistaking opinion for evidence of value. Symptom: “fifteen of twenty shopkeepers said they would use it.” Misunderstanding: that stated intent predicts behaviour. Diagnostic: ask what the shopkeepers gave up, such as a morning, a signed commitment or a first order, because behaviour costs something and opinion does not. Sethi's concierge pilot, in which her team takes orders by phone and delivers them, with 60 stores and a pass mark of 18 (30 per cent), measures a second order, not a sentiment.

Leaving viability to the end. Symptom: a launch date and no unit economics. Misunderstanding: that viability is something finance reviews after the product exists. Diagnostic: build Table 1 for your own product this week; if you cannot, you do not know your viability risk.

Treating one failed test as a verdict on the whole idea. Symptom: killing a product because the first prototype confused users. Misunderstanding: that all four risks are equally fatal. Diagnostic: ask whether the failure is repairable by redesign or lies in want or economics.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Sethi's week looks like this. On Monday she has the four-line version of Figure 1 on one page. By Wednesday finance has given her the real margin and she has Table 1 on the table, with the 4.5 per cent case shown first and not buried. The tests are scheduled by Table 2, each with a written pass mark before it starts: 18 of 60 stores reordering, at least 10 of 12 owners (83 per cent) completing an order unaided, 1,800 of 2,000 line items (90 per cent) transcribed correctly, a cost to serve at or below ₹97.875. With only 12 owners the usability mark catches gross failures, not fine differences. Each owner is named. The budget is released in stages, not as ₹240 lakh on day one, and the board is told which result would stop the project.

9. What Sethi decided

She asked the board on 14 August for ₹9.5 lakh of testing money, not the full build, and committed to returning in six weeks with four results. The viability desk check and the concierge pilot began the following Monday, in parallel, because both were cheap and neither depended on the other; the speech spike waited for the pilot to supply real recordings of how shopkeepers actually speak. Her reasoning was that the budget request was only 3.96 per cent of the total, that the largest exposure per rupee sat in the cheapest test, and that a board which hears “here is what would stop us” trusts the plan more.

What to learn next: riskiest assumption first, which supplies the reasoning behind ranking, then the design of discovery experiments, feasibility spikes, and viability checks across legal, finance, brand and operations. The first tells you how to choose; the others tell you how to run the test once chosen.

Two questions to sit with. Which of the four risks in your current project has no test designed for it, and what does that omission say about who is in the room? And if you had to put a number on your most favoured assumption being false, would your team agree with it, and what would change if you were forced to publish the number?

What Nobody Could Tell Nilakshi Yeolekar

Sunday night, 8 November 2026.

1. The night before

At twenty to eleven on Sunday night, 8 November 2026, Nilakshi Yeolekar sat at her dining table in Baner, Pune, with four documents. Three she had read too often; the fourth was blank.

The first was the report on the eleven-week field pilot of Gathan Shelf: a reusable logger that rides with a crate of Nashik grapes or a can of chilled milk, and a service that turns its temperature record into one number — the shelf life the load has left — put before the buyer's quality desk ahead of the truck. It ended on Sunday 4 October and cost ₹109.87 lakh. The second was a letter of intent from Ghadeer Fresh Markets LLC of Dubai. The third was a half-page from Niranjan Yerunkar, co-founder and chief executive: Board is Friday. One slide by six on Monday. Not options. A direction.

The fourth was her recommendation: a heading with nothing beneath it. Instead she had a list of four things nobody could tell her. Whether any buyer would pay for the number. Whether drivers and clerks could produce it without a Gathan employee in the yard. Whether it could be made accurate enough to act on. And whether, at any price yet discussed, it could carry its cost. Each had a champion inside Gathan with a reason of their own.

2. How Gathan got here

Gathan Labs was founded in Pune in 2017 by Yerunkar, an instrumentation engineer with nine years in milk analysers. Its first product, Gathan Verify, sat at village collection centres, reading fat and solids-not-fat off the analyser and pushing a tamper-evident ledger entry to the cloud.

In March 2021 Gathan won the contract that made it and constrains it. A western-India state dairy federation — the Federation throughout this case — put Verify into what is now 9,400 collection centres. To win it Gathan accepted two clauses: that all Federation quality data reside in a state-hosted data centre and serve no purpose other than servicing the Federation, and that the Federation hold exclusivity over Gathan in cooperative dairy in three states until 31 March 2027. In FY26 that account produced ₹21.6 crore, 40 per cent of Gathan's ₹54.0 crore of revenue (Exhibit 1).

Both bear on Shelf: seven years of labelled quality readings, the obvious training corpus for a spoilage model, sit inside that data centre and on the face of the clause cannot be touched, and the buyers who move the most chilled volume are closed for five months more. On Friday 16 January 2026 the board ring-fenced ₹14 crore of FY27 spending for a second engine: hardware-led margin, revenue from outside India.

3. The industry Shelf would enter

India's cold chain is three markets that barely speak to each other. In organised retail and quick commerce — Reliance Retail, BigBasket, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart — the buyer owns the shelf, writes the specification and deducts against it on arrival. In the mandi trade that moves most Nashik grapes, the load is sold on sight at the Vashi market in Navi Mumbai and the deduction is a negotiation. In cooperative dairy the plant's quality cell is sovereign and the transporter a contractor.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has tightened transport conditions for milk and cut fruit, which turns temperature records into compliance documents, and the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority regime makes a certified trail worth something at the port. Gathan's exposure abroad is thin: Gathan Trace, its pack-house and export-documentation product, runs in Singapore and two Emirates pack-houses, plus Ghadeer.

4. What happened

Nilakshi took new business on Monday 6 April 2026 with a one-line brief and ₹14 crore. The reasoning was inherited: a January 2026 business case rested on three untested assumptions — that a logger would make forty trips before it was lost; that drivers would scan it themselves, so scanning was free; and that a buyer would pay ₹240 a consignment because the deductions avoided were worth more.

Discovery ran from Monday 11 May to Sunday 21 June: forty-four conversations, nineteen with farmer-producer organisations and pack-houses, twelve with transporters, nine with buyers' quality staff, four with exporters. Ekshala Saathi: Which Risk to Test First?

A decision case on the four product risks, set in Pune, October 2026

1. Opening

On the evening of Monday 12 October 2026, Meenal Velingkar sat in a meeting room at Ekshala's Baner office in Pune, a message from the board chair open on her laptop: "Friday 23rd. Tell us which single test you will run first on Saathi, and what result would make you stop." Ekshala's head of product had spent six weeks on Saathi, a voice-first doubt-solving assistant on WhatsApp for students in Class 8 to 12. Three colleagues wanted three different next steps. Diwali fell on 8 November, twenty-seven days away, and the board's decision gate was Friday 20 November. She had eleven days to choose, and the choice was really about which of four things could kill the product.

2. Company background

Ekshala was founded in Pune in 2019 to teach state-board syllabuses in the language students think in. It sells recorded lessons, weekly tests and live revision in Marathi, Hindi and Kannada medium, mostly to families outside the metros. At 30 September 2026 it had 1,42,000 paying subscribers on annual plans of about ₹2,000. Revenue for the year to March 2026 was ₹27.6 crore, the net loss ₹6.4 crore, and cash ₹22 crore.

PhysicsWallah, Vedantu and Unacademy all sell low-priced courses and have added regional-language features. Ekshala's edge is trust among Marathi-medium parents, with content written for the SSC and HSC boards. Payments run on UPI AutoPay under NPCI rules, and online tuition carries 18 per cent GST. Because most users are minors, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires verifiable parental consent.

3. The situation

In August, support tickets showed unresolved doubts were the commonest reason students lapsed. Saathi was the answer: a student records a voice question in Marathi, often mixed with English technical terms, and receives a spoken and written explanation within a minute. It would be an add-on at ₹149 a month, inclusive of GST. The board approved ₹48 lakh through February 2027.

Exhibit 1 sets out the evidence on each risk. Value looked promising but rested on stated intent. In an August survey, 1,200 of 6,000 invited active subscribers responded, a 20 per cent response, and 504 of those 1,200 said they would definitely or probably pay ₹149. That is 42.0 per cent of respondents; if no non-respondent would pay, it is 8.4 per cent of those invited. Respondents reported a median of seven unresolved doubts a week, about thirty a month.

Mihir Vaingankar, the engineering lead in Bengaluru, had run the only hard test. Forty students in five districts each recorded six questions on a rough prototype, and his team judged whether each transcript kept the question intact enough to answer. Exhibit 2 shows the result. Pune students were understood three times in four; Latur students fewer than half the time.

Usability had the thinnest sample. Meher Vernekar, the senior designer in Berlin, had watched 14 students try the WhatsApp flow over video. Nine completed it unaided. Of the other five, three recorded silence because they did not hold the microphone button, and two, on a parent's phone, could not find the chat.

That left viability. Exhibit 3 is Meenal's model. At ₹149 including 18 per cent GST, Ekshala keeps ₹126.27. An automated answer costs ₹2.40 in speech, language-model and WhatsApp fees, and a share of answers goes to a human tutor for review at ₹14 each; the planning assumption was 8 per cent, and Exhibit 3 also tests a 20 per cent stress case. Everything turned on two unmeasured numbers: doubts per student per month, and the review rate.

4. The people

Mayank Valsangkar, head of growth in Pune, wanted to launch. Diwali is when families buy, he argued, forecasting that 10 per cent of subscribers, 14,200 students, would add Saathi. "Nearly everyone said yes in the survey," he told her.

Mihir Vaingankar, in Bengaluru, wanted a feasibility spike first. A product that mishears two questions in five, he said, would cost Ekshala parents' trust.

Meher Vernekar, in Berlin, wanted to watch real students pay for and use a human-run version; she thought the interface problems small and the real question whether anyone returned in week three. Berlin runs 3.5 hours behind India until clocks change on 25 October, then 4.5, so the Monday 4:30 pm IST call is at 1:00 pm for her now and at noon after the change.

Meenal Velingkar owned the decision. She had capacity for exactly one test before 20 November, since the spike and a concierge pilot (Options B and C below) needed the same two engineers.

5. The options

Option A: launch to all subscribers by Friday 6 November. Harden the prototype and message all 1,42,000 subscribers before Diwali, for ₹22 lakh (₹18 lakh engineering, ₹4 lakh campaign). Upside: the Diwali buying window. Cost: if Exhibit 3's 30-doubt, 20 per cent review case holds, 14,200 adopters would bring in ₹17.93 lakh a month after GST against ₹22.15 lakh of answer cost, a monthly loss of ₹4.22 lakh, with transcription errors in front of parents.

Option B: a four-week feasibility spike. Record 1,000 voice questions (100 students, 10 in each of 10 districts, 10 questions each), fine-tune the speech model and measure usable transcription. It costs ₹14 lakh (₹5 lakh recordings, ₹3 lakh compute, ₹6 lakh staff time). Upside: it attacks the weakest measured result and pins down the review rate. Cost: it says nothing about demand, and it ends on the gate date itself.

Option C: a three-week paid concierge pilot. Invite 5,000 random subscribers, take ₹149 from the first 500 who accept, and have human tutors answer their voice notes by hand. It costs ₹6 lakh (₹4.2 lakh tutors, ₹1.8 lakh tooling) and would collect up to ₹74,500 if 500 accept. Upside: it measures real willingness to pay, doubts per month and week-three return. Cost: it proves nothing about the speech technology.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, rank the four risks by the strength of their evidence. Which figures rest on observed behaviour and which on stated intent?

2. In Exhibit 3, which inputs are really outputs of another risk? What review rate does Saathi need to break even at 30 doubts a month?

3. For each option, which risk does it test, what result would change Meenal's plan, and which risks does it leave untouched?

4. Choose one route, write its stop criterion before the test begins, and say what the board should expect on 20 November.

7. A note for the learner

The four risks (value, usability, feasibility, viability) are a sorting device. For each assumption, ask which kind of failure it would be, how strong the evidence is, and what failure would cost. Then test the one most likely to kill the product, soonest and cheapest. Mayank's trap was to let value, evidenced only by stated intent, stand in for all four. Another is fixing what is easy to see: usability had a clear remedy, a prominent record button.

One defensible path is Option B. Exhibit 2 shows a measured accuracy of 57.5 per cent. If every unusable transcript were sent to human review, the review rate would be 42.5 per cent, the cost per doubt ₹8.35, and the contribution at 30 doubts −₹124.23. This assumes the review rate equals the unusable share, a simplification. Break-even at 30 doubts needs a review rate of about 12.9 per cent, so roughly 87.1 per cent usable, while the 8 per cent plan needs 92 per cent. Feasibility therefore sits upstream of viability, and demand cannot rescue a product that costs more to answer than it earns. The stop criterion should be fixed in advance. On those assumptions and 30 doubts, proceed to a pilot at 920 or more usable of 1,000 questions (92 per cent); walk away below 871 (87.1 per cent); between 871 and 919, rework pricing or cap monthly doubts.

Option C is the runner-up and the right next step if the spike passes, so Meenal should give the board a December date for it. Option A launches without any test whose result could have stopped it. The honest costs of B are a missed Diwali window and a result that arrives on the gate day. Both are recoverable; lost trust is not.
